It looks like you've got a Venus Flytrap! Seeing those traps turn black can be alarming, but it’s actually a very common part of their life cycle. Each individual trap can only snap shut about 3–5 times before it dies off to make room for new growth.

Based on the photo, here is a quick assessment and some tips to keep it thriving:

What's Happening with the Black Traps?

  • Natural Lifespan: If the center of the plant is green and pushing out new leaves, the blackening of older, outer traps is completely normal.
  • Digestion Toll: Sometimes a trap turns black after eating a bug that was too large, which causes the trap to rot before it can finish digesting.
  • Acclimation: If you just bought this, it might be reacting to a change in light or humidity.

Care Essentials for Success

Venus Flytraps are notoriously picky because they evolved in very specific bog conditions (specifically the Carolinas in the US).

FactorRequirement
WaterDistilled, rain, or reverse osmosis water only. Tap water contains minerals that will eventually "burn" the roots and kill the plant.
LightThey love direct sunlight (at least 6+ hours). If kept indoors, a very strong grow light is usually necessary.
SoilThey need nutrient-poor, acidic soil—usually a mix of sphagnum peat moss and perlite. Never use standard potting soil or fertilizer.
FeedingDon't force-feed it! It only needs a couple of bugs a month. Never feed it human food (like hamburger meat), as the fats will kill the traps.

Maintenance Tips

  • Trim the dead parts: You can gently snip off the black traps with clean scissors to prevent mold, just be careful not to trigger the healthy green traps.
  • The "Tray Method": Since they are bog plants, keep the pot sitting in a small tray with about a half-inch of distilled water so the moss stays consistently damp.
  • Dormancy: Keep in mind that in the winter, these plants naturally go dormant. They will look a bit "sad" and stop growing for a few months—this is normal and necessary for their long-term health.
